pages.name: Heat and work
pages.text: Heated, a gas can push its piston out. That push is [[work]]. What it does not spend as work, it keeps inside as [[internal energy]]. Here 500 J of heat goes in. At a steady 200 kPa, the gas pushes the piston out 1 L, which is 0.001 m³. The work is 200,000 Pa × 0.001 m³ = 200 J, the shaded area. The [[first law of thermodynamics]] says the rise in internal energy is heat in minus work: 500 − 200 = 300 J.

pages.name: All of it as work
pages.task: A gas takes in 400 J of heat and does 400 J of work. How much does its internal energy change?
pages.why: The rise in internal energy is the heat in minus the work done: 400 − 400 = 0 J. Every joule that came in left again as work.

pages.name: Locked, then pushed
pages.text: Count heat into the gas as plus, and work done by the gas as plus too. Here the piston is locked, and 500 J goes in. The gas cannot move it, so it does no work, and the chart has no area. All 500 J stays, so the internal energy rises 500 J. Then the piston is pushed in. That work is done on the gas, so it counts as minus. Taking off a minus adds, so the internal energy rises further.

pages.name: Pushed in
pages.task: 300 J of work pushes the piston in, and the gas gives out 100 J of heat. What happens to its internal energy?
pages.why: Heat given out counts as minus, so the heat in is −100 J. Work done on the gas counts as minus too, so the work is −300 J. The rise is −100 − (−300) = 200 J. The push put in more than the heat took out.

pages.name: Round a loop
pages.text: An engine runs its gas round a loop. It pushes out while hot. Then it is cooled. Then it is squeezed back while cool, at a lower pressure. So the squeeze takes less work than the push gave. Its internal energy ends where it started. So over each loop, the work out is the heat taken in minus the heat given out. That work is the loop's area. Squeezed hot, the gas would push back as hard, taking back all the work. So no loop can skip the cooling.

pages.name: The exhaust
pages.task: Fuel brings 1,000 kW. The work is 350 kW, and the cooling water carries 300 kW. What does the exhaust carry?
pages.why: Every kilowatt of fuel leaves somewhere. 1,000 − 350 − 300 = 350 kW leaves in the exhaust. People call the cooling and exhaust heat a loss, but nothing is lost. It is [[heat rejected]], carried away, so the three add back to 1,000 kW.

pages.name: Typical work
pages.task: In a typical engine, cooling and exhaust carry 60 to 70% of the fuel. With 1,000 kW of fuel, how much is left as work?
pages.why: 60 to 70% of 1,000 kW is 600 to 700 kW of heat. The work is the rest. That is 1,000 − 700 = 300 kW, up to 1,000 − 600 = 400 kW.

pages.name: The Carnot line
pages.text: No engine working between a hot side and a cold side can beat the [[Carnot limit]], 1 − T cold ÷ T hot, in kelvin. At 800 K and 300 K, that is 1 − 300 ÷ 800 = 62.5%. Work pushed past the line stops there, in red. Only the temperatures move the line. How far it binds a real diesel is debated.

pages.name: A maker's claim
pages.task: A maker claims 75% of its fuel energy as work. The engine's hot side is at 727 °C and its cold side at 27 °C. Is that possible?
pages.why: Put both temperatures in kelvin. 727 + 273 = 1,000 K, and 27 + 273 = 300 K. The limit is 1 − 300 ÷ 1,000 = 70%. A claim of 75% passes it, so it cannot be right.

pages.name: A generator set
pages.text: On a [[generator set]], the engine's work drives an alternator. So the work becomes the [[electrical output]], 350 kW here. The cooling water still carries 300 kW, nearly as much. All of that leaves through the cooler. So size a cooler on the heat the engine rejects to its cooling water. Never size it on the set's rating.

pages.name: Sizing the cooler
pages.task: A generator set gives 400 kW of electrical output. Its output is 40% of its fuel energy. Its cooling carries 30% of the fuel. What must the cooler carry?
pages.why: Find the fuel first. Divide the output by the efficiency: 400 ÷ 0.4 = 1,000 kW. The cooling takes 30% of that, so the cooler must carry 300 kW. That is nearly as much as the output.

pages.name: Seawater flow
pages.task: Seawater must carry that 300 kW away, warming by 10 °C. Each kilogram takes 3,850 J for each °C it warms. What flow does that need?
pages.why: Each kilogram warming 10 °C carries 3,850 × 10 = 38,500 J. The cooler must shed 300 kW, which is 300,000 J each second. So 300,000 ÷ 38,500 is about 7.8 kg of seawater each second.
